llm_response.content:
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
“Peer Effects in Super-market Checkout Lines”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Within-shift event–study Difference-in-Differences (DiD).

Why it fits  
• We observe the exact minute a specific co-worker clocks-in or clocks-out.  
• We compare the focal cashier’s productivity in the same shift immediately before vs. after that moment (first difference) and difference this change across high- vs. low-productivity arrivals (second difference).  
• Rich fixed effects (cashier, date×store×10-minute, lane, etc.) purge time-invariant heterogeneity and common time shocks.  
• The reflection problem is circumvented because the co-worker’s “quality” is measured from her permanent, pre-event productivity (computed on other days).

Formally  

yist = β HighPeerPresentist + γXist + αi + δst + εist,  

and in event-study form  

yist = Σk≠−1 βk 1{τ=k} + αi + δst + εist,  

where τ is ten-minute distance to the arrival of a high-productivity peer that is in the focal cashier’s line of sight.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
HighPeerPresentist = 1 if, at time block t, at least one co-worker with a permanent productivity in the top 25 % of the store distribution is simultaneously on the same shift AND physically visible to cashier i.

Control groups  
A.  Same cashier, same shift, ten-minute cells just before the high-peer arrives (within-shift counterfactual).  
B.  Ten-minute cells in which a low-productivity peer arrives (difference-in-differences across peer quality).  
C.  A triple-diff robustness: visible × high-peer vs. non-visible × high-peer.

Event timing  
Event date τ = 0 is the first 10-minute block after the high-peer clocks in (or clocks out for the departure specification). We use a symmetric window of six cells (±60 minutes).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Scheduling exogeneity: Managers create rosters to satisfy forecast demand, not to mix specific worker types for productivity reasons. Because rosters are planned weeks ahead, the precise event time of any given high-peer arrival is plausibly unrelated to the focal cashier’s transient productivity. Plausibility: High—supported by interviews and scheduling records.

A2. Parallel pre-trends: Absent the arrival of a high peer, the treated and control observations would have followed the same productivity path in the short pre-event window. Plausibility: Testable using event-study leads.

A3. No anticipation within the ±60-minute window: Cashiers do not speed up in expectation of a fast peer who is about to arrive. Plausibility: High—schedule boards are posted but workers usually do not know who will be placed in which lane.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (localized peer effects): The only peer that matters within the window is the arriving cashier; effects do not spill over to other lanes or propagate multiple hops in ten minutes. Plausibility: Moderate—visual line-of-sight restriction helps.

A5. No simultaneous demand shocks differentially correlated with peer quality: Any surge in customers that might alter scanning speed is absorbed by store×date×10-minute fixed effects, so remaining variation comes from peer quality. Plausibility: Reasonably high.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Customer flow shocks. Arrival of an extra cashier—especially a fast one—may coincide with a surge in customers that requires faster scanning.  
• Remedy: Include store×date×10-minute fixed effects so customer traffic that is common to all lanes at that moment is purged. Run placebo that keeps only moments when some peer arrives and compare high-vs-low productivity.

T2. Non-random lane assignment. Fast cashiers might be systematically placed near other fast cashiers or on busy lines.  
• Remedy: Add lane fixed effects and lane×time-of-day fixed effects. In robustness, restrict to cases where the focal cashier stays in the same lane throughout the window.

T3. Reflection (peer influenced by focal). Although we use the peer’s permanent productivity, contemporaneous behavior of the peer might still react to the focal cashier.  
• Remedy: Use only the peer’s average speed calculated on different days to define “high.” Exclude today’s observations from the construction of the peer-quality variable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dim FE estimators
library(ggplot2)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
d <- fread("supermarket_scanner_panel.csv")   # one row = cashier×10-min cell

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct permanent productivity
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
d[, perm_speed := mean(scan_speed), by = .(cashier_id)]
# Compute it leave-one-shift-out
d[, shift_id := paste0(store, "_", date, "_", shift_no)]
d[, perm_speed := mean(scan_speed[shift_id != shift_id[1L]]), 
     by = cashier_id]

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Identify arrivals & departures
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
setorder(d, cashier_id, clock_time)
d[, peer_arrival := (shift_minute == 0)]             # first row in shift
# For each focal cashier and time block, identify visible peers on duty
d[, high_peer_present := 
      as.integer(any(perm_speed > quantile(perm_speed, .75) &
                     on_duty == 1 & visible == 1)), 
      by = .(store, clock_time, focal_cashier = cashier_id)]

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Create event-study window
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# Flag events = first high-peer arrival where previously none
d[, event_id := NA_integer_]
d[, high_peer_lag := shift(high_peer_present, type="lag"), 
     by = cashier_id]
d[, new_event := (high_peer_present == 1 & (is.na(high_peer_lag) | high_peer_lag == 0))]
d[new_event == TRUE, event_id := .I]                  # unique id
d[, event_id := zoo::na.locf(event_id, na.rm = FALSE), 
     by = cashier_id]                                # fill forward
d[, rel_time := as.integer(clock_time - clock_time[new_event == TRUE]),
     by = event_id]

# Keep ±6 ten-minute cells
ev <- d[!is.na(event_id) & abs(rel_time) <= 6]

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Baseline event-study regression
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
est <- feols(scan_speed ~ i(rel_time, ref = -1) | cashier_id +
                store_date_block10 + lane_id, 
             data = ev, cluster = "cashier_id")
etable(est)

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: placebo low-peer arrival
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
d[, low_peer_present := 
      as.integer(any(perm_speed < quantile(perm_speed, .25) &
                     on_duty == 1 & visible == 1)),
      by = .(store, clock_time, cashier_id)]
# Repeat steps above building rel_time_low and rerun regression.

# -----------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Plot event-study coefficients
# -----------------------------------------------------------------
evplot <- broom::tidy(est, conf.int = TRUE)[,.(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)]
evplot <- evplot[grepl("rel_time", term)]
evplot[, k := as.numeric(gsub("i\\(rel_time, ref = -1\\)::", "", term))]
ggplot(evplot, aes(k, estimate)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = .2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() + labs(y = "Δ items/sec", x = "Ten-minute intervals rel. to arrival")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: Positive. Economic intuition suggests social pressure or imitation—seeing a faster co-worker will raise one’s own scanning speed.

Magnitude: Supermarket work is fairly routinised, so large swings are unlikely. A reasonable prior is 0.02–0.04 items/second (≈ 2–3 % of mean speed, or ≈ 0.15 standard deviations) in the first 30–60 minutes after arrival; symmetric negative effect at departure.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD/Event Study)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent)
C1. Pre-trend/parallel trends tested and satisfied …… 1  
C2. No anticipation effects within window ……………… 1  
C3. No composition changes within unit over time …… 1  
C4. No spillovers to control units (SUTVA) ……………… 0  
C5. Correct standard errors & proper clustering ……… 1  

Overall score: 4 / 5. The main concern is residual spillovers across lanes beyond visual line of sight, which we will continue to test in robustness analyses.
